t19: Most party games are written for a crowd; when three people are left, someone says "this won't work for us" and the evening ends with TV. But games for small groups have different rules, not a different game. Below is what works for groups of 2, 3, and 4.
t21: You can't form teams with two people, so the "describe–guess" logic works directly head-to-head. Your opponent is also the guesser; the score is kept accordingly.
t23: One person describes in turns, the other guesses. Keep time and count how many words you get; at the end of the round, compare scores.
t25: Say three sentences about yourself, one of them false. Your opponent tries to find the lie.
t27: Pick a category (movies, cities, brands) and take turns naming things; whoever gets stuck loses.
t29: You both roll; the one with the higher roll picks the task, the other does it.
t30: 3 people: the trickiest but most flexible number
t31: Three people can't be split into teams, which is why this number gets stuck most. The solution is simple:
t33: . Each round, one person describes, one guesses, one referees; roles shift every round.
t34: The describer gets a point, the guesser gets a point, the referee keeps time and follows the rules.
t35: After three rounds, everyone has played each role once; the score is fairly distributed.
t36: If the referee role feels boring, let the referee also be the second guesser, and the first one to get it wins the point.
t38: Four people work for both forming teams and competing individually. In a home setting, this is the most balanced group size.
t40: Classic team setup; change the describer each round.
t42: Everyone keeps their own score, no teams.
t44: Four pieces on the board make a nice race, and turns are quick.
t46: Two matches, the winners play the final. Ends in 20 minutes.

t55: Three rules that keep small-group games alive
t57: With fewer people, turns come faster; 90 seconds feels too long, 45–60 seconds is the right measure.
t59: In a large group 30 points is reasonable, with 2 people 15 is enough — otherwise the game drags and fades.
t61: With fewer people, the same game gets repetitive faster; changing game types every 20 minutes gives much better results than forcing one game longer.

t65: What games do you play at home with 2 people?
t66: Taking turns describing words, Truth or Lie, and sequential category games work very well with two people. Instead of team-based modes, pick head-to-head score racing.
